Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Social Ministry Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Stay Near Exit: make sure to stay close to exit, Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
  Threat: Irritability: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage

Vignette:
Layla, a 51-year-old social ministry worker, presents as a woman holding a lifetime of tension in her shoulders. For decades, she has navigated the world with a quiet, rigid vigilance, but in recent months, the scaffolding she built to contain her past has begun to collapse. The memories, or rather, the sensations of what happened, are not linear narratives from her childhood. She explains that she cannot put the events into words; there is no story to tell, only a visceral imprint of terror. When an image does flash, it is of the heavy oak door in her father’s study clicking shut, the sound echoing louder in her mind now than it did forty years ago. What follows is not a picture, but a feeling—a sudden, crushing weight and the helpless contortion of her own small body. When these moments come upon her, she feels her spine arch and her shoulders hunch involuntarily, her body reenacting a posture of defense she hasn't consciously remembered for years. This bodily memory is inevitably followed by a surge of pure, hot rage that leaves her trembling and breathless, furious at a ghost she can never confront.

This internal world has long dictated the shape of her external one. At her church ministry, where she is meant to offer counsel and support, her primary focus has become managing the environment. In staff meetings, she positions her chair closest to the door, a silent sentinel guarding her own escape. She has become an expert at orchestrating conversations in the open-plan kitchen or bustling reception area, doing anything to avoid the quiet intimacy of a private office. She is certain that being alone with another person behind a closed door is the most dangerous situation imaginable. This has not gone unnoticed. Her colleagues have begun to see her as evasive, and clients who need confidentiality feel put off by her insistence on public spaces. The work she once found deeply meaningful now feels like a minefield.

The sense of imminent threat is not confined to her office. Walking from the parking lot to her apartment building is a nightly ordeal. Layla finds herself constantly glancing over her shoulder, her keys clenched in her fist, convinced that the sound of footsteps half a block away belongs to someone following her. The world is filled with false alarms that her body treats as real. A car door slamming down the street sends a jolt of adrenaline through her; a friendly parishioner tapping her on the shoulder to say hello can cause her to gasp and flinch away. The constant state of hyperarousal leaves her nerves frayed, and the slightest frustration can detonate into a disproportionate outburst. Last week, she screamed at a teenage grocery clerk for packing her bread under a can of soup, her anger so sudden and fierce that it frightened them both. The shame that followed was immediate and crushing.

Over the last six months, the avoidance has escalated. The thought of her calendar, filled with one-on-one client appointments in small, enclosed rooms, has become unbearable. She has started calling in sick on days when her schedule is particularly dense, citing migraines she doesn't have. The pile of unfinished case files on her desk grows, a monument to the clients she feels she is failing. The final impetus for seeking help came two weeks ago, when her supervisor called her in for a formal performance review. With the door closed, Layla could barely hear the words over the frantic pounding in her chest. The supervisor spoke of missed appointments and a pattern of avoiding client-facing duties. It was the ultimate humiliation: her life’s work was to create safety for others, yet she could not feel safe herself. She is here now, exhausted and terrified, hoping to find a way to exist in a room with another person without her body screaming that she is about to die.
